metadata.title: Conceptual inconsistencies in finite-dimensional quantum and classical mechanics

extraction_notes.note: Numbered equations (1) and (5)-(6) retyped as external theorems because the text names them as results (Weyl's demonstration; the Ehrenfest theorems).
definition or remark: the sentence both asserts that the eigenbases are mutually unbiased and explains the term; kept as an external definition.

Eqs. (7)-(8) and (15) are derived in prose by applying ODM to the Ehrenfest theorems, but the derivation sentence contains the equation and an equation is not a result, so no proof node was made; the dependency is recorded as uses edges from the Ehrenfest theorems and ODM.
One sentence introduces two symbols (H_mub^star and H_mub); a sentence cannot be split, so one definition node carries both.
The numerical evidence (spectra and twentieth eigenvectors) is only in the figures, whose content is not extractable; the claims rest on them.
The Introduction's and Outlook's summary sentences restating the paper's findings, and the numerical parameter-selection recipe, were left out as non-statement discussion.

nodes.name: Weyl's relation
nodes.statement: \left| \langle x \ket{p} \right|^2 = \mbox{const} \Longleftrightarrow \commut{ \hat{x}, \hat{p} } = i \hbar,
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
nodes.statement_short: Constant overlap modulus between position and momentum eigenstates is equivalent to the canonical commutation relation.
conclusions: \left| \langle x \ket{p} \right|^2 = \mbox{const} \Longleftrightarrow \commut{ \hat{x}, \hat{p} } = i \hbar
nodes.label: PhysOrigin_CCR

nodes.name: Nonexistence of bounded operators obeying the canonical commutation relation
nodes.statement: The left-hand side of Eq. (\ref{PhysOrigin_CCR}) is well defined in a finite-dimensional space, whereas the right-hand side of Eq. (\ref{PhysOrigin_CCR}) is not because no bounded operators obey the canonical commutation relation \cite{Weyl1950, Reed1980}.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
nodes.statement_short: The CCR side of Weyl's relation has no finite-dimensional meaning since no bounded operators satisfy the CCR.
conclusions: no bounded operators obey the canonical commutation relation

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional coordinate and momentum operators
nodes.statement: Thus, in the literature on finite-dimensional quantum mechanics, the coordinate and momentum operators are usually defined as those whose eigenvectors obey \begin{align} \langle x_n \ket{p_k} = \exp(i2\pi n k /N) / \sqrt{N}, \end{align} where $n,k = -j, -j+1, \ldots, j-1, j$, $j =2N+1$, $\hat{x} \ket{x_n} = an\ket{x_n}$, $\hat{p} \ket{p_k} = 2\pi \hbar k/(aN) \ket{p_k}$, and $N$ is the Hilbert space's dimension (see Ref. \cite{DelaTorre2003a} for a detailed description of the notation).
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
nodes.origin_citation: de la Torre & Goyeneche 2003 (and finite-dimensional QM literature)
nodes.statement_short: Finite-dimensional position and momentum operators are defined by eigenbases related by a discrete Fourier transform.

nodes.name: Mutually unbiased bases
nodes.statement: According to Eq. (\ref{Deff_PX_as_MUBS}), the coordinate and momentum eigenvectors form mutually unbiased bases, which means that if a system is prepared in a state from one of the bases, then all outcomes of the measurement with respect to the other basis are equally probable.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
differentia: if a system is prepared in a state from one of the bases, then all outcomes of the measurement with respect to the other basis are equally probable
nodes.statement_short: Coordinate and momentum eigenbases are mutually unbiased: a state from one basis gives uniform outcomes in the other.

nodes.name: Operational Dynamic Modeling (ODM)
nodes.statement: To answer this question, we employ Operational Dynamic Modeling (ODM) \cite{Bondar2011c}, a universal and systematic framework for deriving equations of motion from the evolution of the dynamical average values.

nodes.name: ODM derivation of the Liouville and Schrodinger equations from the Ehrenfest theorems
nodes.statement: In Ref. \cite{Bondar2011c}, along with a number of other applications, we utilized this method to infer the classical Liouville and Schr\"{o}dinger equations from the Ehrenfest theorems, \begin{align} m\frac{d}{dt} \bra{\Psi(t)} \hat{x} \ket{\Psi(t)} & = \bra{\Psi(t)} \hat{p} \ket{\Psi(t)}, \\ \frac{d}{dt} \bra{\Psi(t)} \hat{p} \ket{\Psi(t)} & = \bra{\Psi(t)} -U'(\hat{x}) \ket{\Psi(t)}, \end{align} by assuming that the coordinate $\hat{x}$ and momentum $\hat{p}$ commuted in the former case and obeyed the canonical commutation relation in the latter.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
nodes.statement_short: ODM yields the classical Liouville equation from the Ehrenfest theorems with commuting x,p, and the Schrodinger equation under the CCR.
assumptions: by assuming that the coordinate $\hat{x}$ and momentum $\hat{p}$ commuted in the former case and obeyed the canonical commutation relation in the latter
conclusions: we utilized this method to infer the classical Liouville and Schr\"{o}dinger equations from the Ehrenfest theorems

nodes.name: Commutator equations have no non-trivial finite-dimensional solution
nodes.statement: We shall demonstrate below that Eqs. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) cannot be satisfied by non-trivial finite-dimensional operators.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
conclusions: cannot be satisfied by non-trivial finite-dimensional operators

nodes.name: Nonexistence of the free particle in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics
nodes.statement: Assume $\hat{p}$ and $\hat{H}$ are non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators. If $\commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{p} } = 0$ then there is no finite-dimensional linear operator $\hat{x}$ such that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: If finite-dimensional Hermitian H and p commute and are nonzero, no finite-dimensional x satisfies i[H,x]=p.
assumptions: Assume $\hat{p}$ and $\hat{H}$ are non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators.
conclusions: there is no finite-dimensional linear operator $\hat{x}$ such that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$
nodes.label: NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Let $\ket{E_n}$ denote a joint eigenvector of $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{p}$ such that $\hat{H} \ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$ and $\hat{p} \ket{E_n} = p_n \ket{E_n}$. Assuming that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$, one obtains \begin{align} i \bra{E_n} \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } \ket{E_m} = i (E_n - E_m) \bra{E_n} \hat{x} \ket{E_m} = p_m \langle E_n \ket{E_m}, \end{align} $\forall n,m$. The special case of this identity, when $n=m$, reads $p_m = 0$, $\forall m$. This contradicts the assumption that $\hat{p}$ is a non-zero matrix.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: take matrix elements of i[H,x]=p in a joint eigenbasis of H and p; diagonal elements force p=0.

Assuming that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$, one obtains \begin{align} i \bra{E_n} \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } \ket{E_m} = i (E_n - E_m) \bra{E_n} \hat{x} \ket{E_m} = p_m \langle E_n \ket{E_m}, \end{align} $\forall n,m$.

nodes.name: Nonexistence of the free particle in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics (physical implication)
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem} physically implies the nonexistence of the ``free'' particle in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
conclusions: the nonexistence of the ``free'' particle in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics

nodes.name: Probability-conservation argument for the nonexistence of the free particle
nodes.statement: This statement is also a consequence of probability conservation, closely linked to Stone's theorem. If the wave function's normalization is constant and $\hat{x}$ is finite-dimensional, then the particle's motion is confined to the spatial interval bound by the smallest and largest eigenvalues of $\hat{x}$. This confinement must be realized by some force.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Conservation of normalization with finite-dimensional x confines the particle between extreme eigenvalues, requiring a confining force.

nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Constant norm and finite-dimensional x confine the particle to a bounded interval.

nodes.name: Confining force
nodes.statement: This confinement must be realized by some force.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: The confinement requires a force, so the particle is not free.

nodes.name: Confining force
nodes.statement: Since standalone Eq. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) is solvable with respect to $\hat{H}$ [see Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) below], then $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{p} }/\hbar$ from Eq. (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) can be taken as the definition of this confining force.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: The confining force is defined as i[H,p]/hbar with H solving the first commutator equation.

nodes.name: Ehrenfest theorems fail for a particle in a box
nodes.statement: Note that the Ehrenfest theorems do not hold for a particle in a box even in the infinite-dimensional case \cite{Alonso2000}.

conclusions: the Ehrenfest theorems do not hold for a particle in a box even in the infinite-dimensional case

nodes.name: No finite-dimensional differentiation as a commutator
nodes.statement: There are no finite-dimensional operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ such that \begin{align} \commut{ f(\hat{A}), \hat{B} } = f'(\hat{A}) \end{align} for any ``good'' function $f(z)$.

nodes.statement_short: No finite-dimensional operators A,B make commutation with B act as differentiation on functions of A.
conclusions: There are no finite-dimensional operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ such that
nodes.label: NoDiffAsCommutator_Theorem

nodes.name: Commutator as derivative
nodes.statement: \commut{ f(\hat{A}), \hat{B} } = f'(\hat{A})
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.label: NoDiffAsCommutator_Eq1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let a function of an operator be defined as (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Nazaikinskii1992}) \begin{align} f(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \quad f'(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int ik g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \notag \end{align} where $g(k)$ is the Fourier transform of a function $f(z)$. The correctness of Eq. (\ref{NoDiffAsCommutator_Eq1}) implies \begin{align} \commut{ e^{ik\hat{A}}, \hat{B} } = ik e^{ik\hat{A}}. \end{align} Differentiating the last identity with respect to $k$ and setting $k=0$, we reach the contradiction $\commut{ \hat{A}, \hat{B} } = 1$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction via Fourier representation of operator functions: the identity for exponentials, differentiated at k=0, gives [A,B]=1.

nodes.name: Commutator identity for operator exponentials

nodes.statement_short: The assumed identity yields the commutator relation for exponentials.

nodes.name: Differentiate at k=0

nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
nodes.statement_short: Differentiating in k at k=0 gives [A,B]=1, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Nonsolvability of the second commutator equation and two nonequivalent force definitions
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{NoDiffAsCommutator_Theorem} establishes not only the nonsolvability of Eq. (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) but also two nonequivalent definitions ($\hat{F} = - U'(\hat{x})$ and $\hat{F} = i\commut{U(\hat{x}), \hat{p}}/\hbar$) of a potential force $\hat{F}$ in a finite-dimensional framework.

nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2 implies the second commutator equation is unsolvable and that -U'(x) and i[U(x),p]/hbar are inequivalent force definitions.
conclusions: the nonsolvability of Eq. (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian})

nodes.name: Most general Hamiltonian solving the first commutator equation
nodes.statement: Assuming $\hat{x}$ is Hermitian and has a non-degenerate spectrum, the solution of Eq. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) is \begin{align} \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star} \ket{x_l} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} U(x_k) + C & \mbox{if } k=l \\ \frac{i \hbar \bra{x_k} \hat{p} \ket{x_l} }{m(x_k - x_l)} &\mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right. \end{align} where $\hat{x} \ket{x_l} = x_l \ket{x_l}$ and $C$ is an arbitrary real constant.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.statement_short: For Hermitian x with nondegenerate spectrum, the first commutator equation fixes H's off-diagonal elements in x's eigenbasis; diagonal is U(x_k)+C.
assumptions: Assuming $\hat{x}$ is Hermitian and has a non-degenerate spectrum
$\hat{x} \ket{x_l} = x_l \ket{x_l}$ and $C$ is an arbitrary real constant
conclusions: \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star} \ket{x_l} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} U(x_k) + C & \mbox{if } k=l \\ \frac{i \hbar \bra{x_k} \hat{p} \ket{x_l} }{m(x_k - x_l)} &\mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right.

nodes.name: Ehrenfest-compatible Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star} \ket{x_l} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} U(x_k) + C & \mbox{if } k=l \\ \frac{i \hbar \bra{x_k} \hat{p} \ket{x_l} }{m(x_k - x_l)} &\mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.label: Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian

nodes.name: Generality of the Ehrenfest-compatible Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: For any definition of the momentum operator $\hat{p}$, Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) provides the most general Hamiltonian obeying the first Ehrenfest theorem [Eq. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1})].
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
assumptions: For any definition of the momentum operator $\hat{p}$
conclusions: provides the most general Hamiltonian obeying the first Ehrenfest theorem

nodes.name: Finite-difference momentum operator
nodes.statement: Choosing $\hat{x}$ with equally spaced eigenvalues (with the step $a$) and utilizing the approximation $d \Psi(x_k) /dx \approx [ \Psi(x_{k+1}) - \Psi(x_{k-1}) ] / (2a)$, we can define the momentum operator: $\bra{x_k} \hat{p}_{fd} \ket{x_l} = -i\hbar\left( \delta_{l,k+1} - \delta_{l,k-1} \right)/(2a)$.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
nodes.statement_short: Momentum defined by the central-difference derivative on an equally spaced grid with step a.

nodes.name: Ehrenfest-compatible finite-difference Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: Then, the corresponding Hamiltonian from Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}), \begin{align} \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star}_{fd} \ket{x_l} = \frac{-\hbar^2}{2ma^2} \left( \delta_{l,k+1} + \delta_{l,k-1} \right) + [U(x_k) + C]\delta_{l,k}, \end{align} satisfying the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}), takes the form of the simplest finite-difference approximation for the differential operator: $-\hbar^2/(2m) d^2/dx^2 + U(x)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: First, we employ the Rosenblum theorem \cite{Rosenblum1956} (see Theorem 9.3 in Ref. \cite{Bhatia1997}) to Eq. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and then employ Eq. (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) to show \begin{align} im\hat{x} =& \frac{\hbar}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} d\xi ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} - \xi )^{-1} \hat{p} ( \hat{H} - \xi )^{-1} \notag\\ =& \frac{\hbar}{2\pi i} \hat{p} \oint_{\Gamma} d\xi ( \hat{H} - \xi )^{-2} = 0, \end{align} where $\Gamma$ denotes a union of closed contours in the complex plane with total winding numbers $1$ around $\sigma(\hat{H}^{\dagger})$ and $0$ around $\sigma(\hat{H})$.

ii) $\lim_{t \to +\infty} \left| \langle \Psi(t) \ket{\Psi(t)} \right| < \infty$, where $\ket{\Psi(t)}$ is a solution of Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form})
iii) the eigenvectors $\{ \ket{E_n} \}_{n=1}^N$ ($\hat{H}\ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$, $n \in I \coloneqq \{1,2,\ldots,N\}$) span the entire Hilbert space

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Suppose $\hat{p} \neq 0$. According to Lyapunov stability theory \cite{Lyapunov1992}, the second assumption implies that $\Im(E_n) \leqslant 0$, $\forall n\in I$. Lemma \ref{NonHermitian_Lemma1} guarantees that $\hat{H}$ has at least a single real eigenvalue. Introduce $R \coloneqq \{ n \in I \, | \, \Im(E_n) = 0 \} \neq \emptyset$ -- the set of the real eigenvalues' indices. ``Sandwiching'' Eqs. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) leads to \begin{align} & im ( E_k^* - E_l ) \bra{E_k} \hat{x} \ket{E_l} = \hbar \bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l}, \\ & ( E_k^* - E_l ) \bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l} = 0, \qquad \forall k,l \in I. \end{align} According to Eq. (\ref{NonHermTh1_Eq2}), $\bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l}$ may be non-zero only for $(k,l) \in Q \coloneqq \{ (k,l) \in R \times R \, | \, E_k = E_l \}$. However, Eq. (\ref{NonHermTh1_Eq1}) enforces $\bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l} = 0$, $\forall (k,l) \in Q$. Therefore, we reach the contradiction $\hat{p} = 0$.

nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: Lyapunov stability bounds Im(E_n), Lemma 1 gives a real eigenvalue, and sandwiching the operator equations in H's eigenbasis forces every matrix element of p to vanish.

nodes.name: No free particle in non-Hermitian quantum and classical mechanics
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{NonHermitian_Theorem1}, being a generalization of Theorems \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem} and \ref{NoFiniteDimClassicalMecahnics}, disproves the existence of the free quantum and classical particle within a non-Hermitian setting.

conclusions: disproves the existence of the free quantum and classical particle within a non-Hermitian setting

nodes.name: Circumventing the no-go theorems via nonstandard analysis
nodes.statement: In particular, a key element in proving theorems \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem} and \ref{NoFiniteDimClassicalMecahnics} is the non-existence of a finite real number $r$ such that $0\cdot r \neq 0$. However, this equation has a solution if infinitesimal and infinitely-large numbers are included into the set of real numbers. Thus, some of the no-go theorems may be avoided by utilizing nonstandard analysis \cite{robert2003nonstandard, Almeida2004}, where such extensions are rigorously implemented.
nodes.section: 6 Outlook
nodes.statement_short: The no-go proofs hinge on 0*r=0 for finite reals; nonstandard analysis with infinitesimals and infinities might avoid them.
